plan.topic_summary: Co-packaged optics (CPO) integrates optical transceivers directly onto the same package or substrate as the compute ASIC, potentially reducing power and increasing bandwidth density for data center and AI cluster interconnects. Understanding its technical maturity, cost trajectory, and competitive positioning relative to pluggable optics is critical for a 1–5 year view on networking and interconnect value chains.

How does CPO compare to advanced pluggable optics (e.g., 1.6T, 3.2T) on total cost of ownership, power per bit, and reliability at data center scale over the next 1–3 years?
What are the key manufacturing and packaging barriers (yield, test, repair) that could delay or limit CPO volume production, and how are they being addressed?
What is the expected power and thermal envelope of CPO solutions relative to the ASIC, and does this create a net system-level power advantage or a new bottleneck?

Over a 3–5 year horizon, what alternative interconnect approaches (e.g., advanced copper, near-packaged optics, new electrical signaling standards) could displace or coexist with CPO, and what market share scenarios are plausible?

sources.title: Co-packaged optics (CPO): status, challenges, and solutions
sources.abstract: Due to the rise of 5G, IoT, AI, and high-performance computing applications, datacenter traffic has grown at a compound annual growth rate of nearly 30%. Furthermore, nearly three-fourths of the datacenter traffic resides within datacenters. The conventional pluggable optics increases at a much slower rate than that of datacenter traffic. The gap between application requirements and the capability of conventional pluggable optics keeps increasing, a trend that is unsustainable. Co-packaged optics (CPO) is a disruptive approach to increasing the interconnecting bandwidth density and energy efficiency by dramatically shortening the electrical link length through advanced packaging and co-optimization of electronics and photonics. CPO is widely regarded as a promising solution for future datacenter interconnections, and silicon platform is the most promising platform for large-scale integration. Leading international companies (e.g., Intel, Broadcom and IBM) have heavily investigated in CPO technology, an inter-disciplinary research field that involves photonic devices, integrated circuits design, packaging, photonic device modeling, electronic-photonic co-simulation, applications, and standardization. This review aims to provide the readers a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art progress of CPO in silicon platform, identify the key challenges, and point out the potential solutions, hoping to encourage collaboration between different research fields to accelerate the development of CPO technology.

sources.title: Progress in Research on Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: In the 5G era, the demand for high-bandwidth computing, transmission, and storage has led to the development of optoelectronic interconnect technology. This technology has evolved from traditional board-edge optical modules to smaller and more integrated solutions. Co-packaged optics (CPO) has evolved as a solution to meet the growing demand for data. Compared to typical optoelectronic connectivity technology, CPO presents distinct benefits in terms of bandwidth, size, weight, and power consumption. This study presents an overview of CPO, highlighting its fundamental principles, advantages, and distinctive features. Additionally, it examines the current research progress of two distinct approaches utilizing Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Laser (VCSEL) and silicon photonics integration technology. Additionally, it provides a concise overview of the many application situations of CPO. Expanding on this, the analysis focuses on the CPO using 2D, 2.5D, and 3D packaging techniques. Lastly, taking into account the present technological environment, the scientific obstacles encountered by CPO are analyzed, and its future progress is predicted.

sources.title: Co-packaged Optics
Glass Substrate for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics leads to significant power reduction by placing the electronic and photonic chiplets in a single package. An integrated electro-optical substrate made of glass with optical waveguides, through vias and electrical redistribution layers inside a single-sided cavity enables fine-line electrical routing and low-cost assembly. Existing glass and thin film technologies were evaluated and combined into a single process stream including photonic assembly. Photonic chips with silicon nitride waveguides were optically coupled to integrated low-loss (<0.1 dB/cm) glass waveguides with minimum loss of 0.65 dB achieved by fiducial alignment and pick-and-place assembly.

sources.title: Glass Platform for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
sources.abstract: Placing the electrical and photonic chiplets in a single package leads to significant power reduction. Chiplets are connected by fine-line electrical routing over a length of a few millimeters and optical interconnects in the package connect photonic chips with optical fibers for off-package communication. A packaging substrate made of glass with optical waveguides, through glass vias and electrical redistribution layers inside a single-sided cavity enables lower-cost assembly. A single-sided 50 μm deep cavity was etched in glass, and electrical copper lines with 5 μm in height and width were deposited on the floor of the cavity. Ion-exchange (IOX) waveguides with propagation loss of <0.1 dB/cm were fabricated below the glass surface. For flip-chip assembly of photonic chips and optical coupling with the IOX waveguides at the top surface of the glass, all electrical interconnects were located inside the cavity. Photonic chips with silicon nitride waveguides were optically coupled to glass waveguides with a minimum loss of 0.5 dB, achieved by fiducial-aligned flip-chip photonic assembly. A low-profile fiber connector with height of 4.4 mm connects the integrated ion-exchanged waveguides with the optical fibers. Average connector loss of 0.83 dB was demonstrated with physical contact between fibers and IOX glass waveguides.

sources.title: Heterogeneous Integration in Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems
sources.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) and Large Language Model (LLM) require data center to have higher bandwidth, and better energy efficiency. To achieve this, Co-packaged optics (CPO) is one of the future directions that leverages advanced packaging with integrated photonics. However, this tight integration complicates data center system design and multi-physics interactions, including electrical, optical, thermal, mechanical, and material aspects. In this paper, heterogeneous integration (HI) in CPO is discussed. Multi-physics packaging is exemplified with two cases. Challenges in HI technologies are reviewed and corresponding mitigation methods are provided, including (1) thermal crosstalk within the electrical domain and between the electrical and the optical interaction, (2) SIPI of wide-and-slow and narrow-and-fast channel links, and (3) pros and cons of interposer material. Integrated photonics part is introduced and is composed of (1) light sources, (2) optical coupling strategies, (3) fiber attach schemes with advanced packaging, and (4) integrated optical technologies, e.g. novel microlens, optical TSV, 3D waveguide, and optical 3DIC. This article aims to identify the key HI challenges in CPO and points out the potential solutions for future CPO system advancement.

sources.title: Co-Packaged Optics Opportunities in Radio-Access Networks
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics is an emerging technology with the potential to play a key role in 6G radio-access networks, due to its ability to enable high capacity at low energy consumption. Creating a version of the technology that is suitable for radio applications will, however, require some dedicated development to address network characteristics.

sources.title: Perspectives for Co-Packaged Optics in Radio Access Networks
sources.venue: International Conference on Transparent Optical Networks
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics (CPO) is an emerging technology providing optical interconnections with a bandwidth density of the order of Terabit/s per square millimeter. All current development and standardization efforts focus on data centers, to connect very high-capacity switches while improving energy efficiency and footprint compared to designs based on front-panel pluggable optics. We think CPO will have an important role also in 6G networks, to meet the demand for high capacity at low energy consumption. This paper illustrates use cases and requirements for CPO natively designed for radio applications and outlines standardization and industrialization paths

sources.title: Polymer Waveguides for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: This paper demonstrates a low-loss photo patternable polymer waveguide material platform based on benzocyclobutene (BCB) that works in both liquid resins and dry film formats. By precise control of molecule design and refractive index between the core and clad layers, we minimized material absorption at target wavelengths, achieving a propagation loss value of <0.1 dB/cm at 850 nm and <0.3 dB/cm at 1310 nm at the system level based on cutback measurements. We patterned these waveguides on silicon and PCB substrates with laser direct imaging (LDI) or mask aligner, with sub-10 μm accuracy. Moreover, our patterned waveguides maintain thermal stability, with <±5% change in optical loss after multiple reflow processes and 1000 h at 85 °C and 85% humidity (HAST) tests. Lastly, we introduce our modeling framework, predicting transmission, mode profile, and optimal performance of waveguides while considering varying geometries, coupling designs, bend radii, and pitch sizes.

sources.title: Heterogeneous Integration Technology Drives the Evolution of Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and high-performance computing (HPC) has increased the demand for large bandwidth, high energy efficiency, and high-density optical interconnects. Co-packaged optics (CPO) technology offers a promising solution by integrating photonic integrated circuits (PICs) directly within or close to electronic integrated circuit (EIC) packages. This paper explores the evolution of CPO performance from various perspectives, including fan-out wafer level packaging (FOWLP), through-silicon via (TSV)-based packaging, through-glass via (TGV)-based packaging, femtosecond laser direct writing waveguides, ion-exchange glass waveguides, and optical coupling. Micro ring resonators (MRRs) are a high-density integration solution due to their compact size, excellent energy efficiency, and compatibility with CMOS processes. However, traditional thermal tuning methods face limitations such as high static power consumption and severe thermal crosstalk. To address these issues, non-volatile neuromorphic photonics has made breakthroughs using phase-change materials (PCMs). By combining the integrated storage and computing capabilities of photonic memory with the efficient optoelectronic interconnects of CPO, this deep integration is expected to work synergistically to overcome material, integration, and architectural challenges, driving the development of a new generation of computing hardware with high energy efficiency, low latency, and large bandwidth.

sources.title: Reflowable Ceramics Multifiber Ferrule for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: International Conference on Electronics Packaging and iMAPS All Asia Conference (ICEP-IAAC)
sources.abstract: One of the most essential components for Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) is the optical connector ferrule with reflow compatibility. We are developing and evaluating reflow compatible Ceramics Multifiber Ferrule (CMF), which does not suffer any ferrule deformation, fiber pistoning, and performance deterioration even after exposure to more than 260°C environment.

sources.abstract: We demonstrate an uncooled pigtailed-QSFP ELS employing an 8-channel (4-λ × 2) CWDM TOSA for Co-Packaged Optics. When operating 100 mW for all 8 channels, the ELS achieves a record high power conversion efficiency of 14.3 % at a housing temperature of 55 °C.

High Density Integration of Silicon Photonic Chiplets for 51.2T Co-packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: This paper shows the high-density integration of CMOS based silicon photonic chiplets to achieve an optical engine bandwidth of 6.4Tb/s and deliver an all-optical 51.2Tb/s co-packaged optics (CPO) switch solution. An industry first prototype system by co-packaging eight engines with switch die that can deliver double the bandwidth of a 25.6Tb/s solution.

sources.title: A study of lithography process comparison for Co-Package Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: We extracted factors to consider when fabricating devices for Co-Packaged Optics application using semiconductor lithography equipment and compared their strengths and weaknesses to provide guidelines for selecting fine processing tools. We presented SEM images of line patterns using not only conventional exposure tools such as i-line steppers and KrF scanners, but also a nanoimprint lithography tool, and when comparing pattern fidelity with an emphasis on the line edge roughness, the high pattern fidelity of nanoimprint lithography was shown to be remarkably superior. In addition, a comprehensive consideration was given to factors other than resolution, such as line edge roughness, pattern flexibility, cost advantages, and power consumption. As a result, nanoimprint lithography was found to share advantages in patterning in silicon waveguides.

sources.title: Simulation and experimental investigation of liquid-cooling thermal management for high-bandwidth co-packaged optics
sources.abstract: This study explores the application of cold plate liquid cooling technology in co-packaged optics (CPO). By integrating optical modules and the switch chip on the same substrate, CPO shortens the electrical interconnection distance, effectively solving the problems of high power consumption and poor signal integrity of traditional pluggable optical modules under high bandwidth. However, the surge in power density and the thermal crosstalk resulting from high integration density make thermal management one of the key challenges that constrain the reliability of high-capacity co-packaged optics. For the unique architecture of CPO, this study analyzes its heat dissipation needs in detail, and a thermal management scheme is designed. The thermal management scheme is simulated and optimized based on the Navier-Stokes equation. The simulation results show that, in a 51.2 Tbit/s CPO system, the junction temperature of the switch chip is 97.3 °C, the maximum junction temperature of the optical modules is 31.3 °C, and the temperature difference between the optical modules is 2.4 °C to 1.2 °C. To verify the simulation results, a thermal test experimental platform is built, and the experimental results show that the temperature simulation difference is within 4% and the pressure change trend is consistent with the simulation. Combining the experimental data and simulation results, the designed heat sink can satisfy the heat dissipation demands of the 51.2 Tbit/s bandwidth CPO system. This conclusion demonstrates the potential of liquid-cooling technology in CPO, providing support for research on liquid-cooling technology in the CPO. The design provides a theoretical and practical basis for the high performance and reliability of optoelectronic integration technology in wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) systems and micro-ring device applications, contributing to the application of next-generation optical communication networks.

sources.title: Unlocking the Potential of Co-Packaged Optics in AI and HPC: Opportunities and Challenges
sources.abstract: The rapid expansion of AI and high-performance computing is driving unprecedented demand for high-bandwidth, energy-efficient data transmission in data centers. Conventional pluggable optics face limitations in power, latency, and density, prompting the emergence of Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) as a transformative solution. By integrating photonics with ASICs, CPO significantly reduces power consumption and enhances bandwidth scalability. This article reviews recent advancements in CPO, explores key challenges in design, manufacturing, thermal management, and reliability, and compares CPO with Near-Packaged Optics (NPO). It highlights ongoing standardization efforts and underscores CPO's potential to revolutionize next-generation AI and data center interconnect architectures.

sources.title: 3D Optoelectronics and Co-Packaged Optics: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Trends
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics (CPO) and three-dimensional (3D) optoelectronics represent a new frontier in high-speed data communication, targeting the rising demands for bandwidth, energy efficiency, and low latency in data centers, artificial intelligence (AI), and high-performance computing (HPC). This review examines the progression from pluggable optics to integrated photonic solutions, highlighting breakthroughs in silicon photonics, heterogeneous integration, and advanced packaging methods such as 2.5D interposers, Embedded Multi-die Inter- connect Bridge (EMIB), and 3D stacking. These innovations promise significant reductions in power consumption and notable gains in bandwidth density, yet thermal management, manufacturing yields, and alignment precision remain key challenges. Applications span hyperscale data centers, quantum networks, automotive lidar, and aerospace communications, illustrating the wide-reaching impact of these emerging technologies. The paper concludes by emphasizing future research directions and collaborative efforts needed to address remaining barriers and fully harness the transformative potential of integrated photonic- electronic systems.

sources.title: 3D optoelectronics and co-packaged optics: when solving the wrong problems stalls deployment
sources.abstract: The rapid growth of AI and accelerator-driven workloads is forcing a fundamental rethinking of optical interconnect architectures in datacenters. Co-packaged optics and three-dimensional photonic integration have emerged as promising solutions to overcome the energy and bandwidth limitations of electrical I/O. Yet, as optics move closer to compute, packaging, thermal management, and system-level robustness increasingly dominate performance and scalability. Here, we argue that co-packaged optics should not be viewed as a component-level optimization, but as an architectural commitment that reshapes the boundaries between photonics, electronics, and system design. We examine how heterogeneous integration strategies, chiplet-based optics, and emerging packaging platforms redefine scaling laws for AI systems, often introducing trade-offs that are underappreciated in device-centric analyses. Looking forward, we discuss why standardization, serviceability, and thermal-aware co-design will be decisive in determining whether co-packaged optics can transition from early deployment to widespread adoption in AI-scale datacenters.

sources.venue: International Conference on Electronic Packaging Technology (ICEPT)
sources.abstract: With the rise of machine learning and artificial intelligence, data center power usage has increased continuously in recent years, and the bandwidth demand for switches continues to grow. As a result, the traditional pluggable optical modules with high latency and low signal quality can no longer meet the demands of bandwidth growth. As a result, co-packaged optics (CPO) technology has emerged. However, CPO introduces many new challenges, one of which is thermal management. This article explores the liquid-cooling heat dissipation technology for CPO systems over 12.8 Tbps. We designed a heat dissipation structure to address the special heat dissipation needs of CPO systems and verified the structure's excellent performance through simulation and experiment. The simulation value is reasonable and fits the experimental results. At 290W input power, the measured junction temperature of the ASIC is 51 °C, and the temperatures of the 16 optical chips ranged from 28 °C to 29 °C, with a maximum temperature difference of 0.6 °C, demonstrating the efficiency and reliability of this design.

sources.title: Thermal management in copackaged optics: from device assembly to system operation
sources.abstract: The rapid surge in global data traffic, driven by artificial intelligence and hyperscale data centers, has established copackaged optics (CPO) as a pivotal technology for next-generation high-bandwidth and low-power interconnects. By integrating optical engines directly with application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) on a single substrate, CPO significantly reduces electrical link lengths and power consumption. However, the extreme power density of ASICs, together with the temperature sensitivity of photonic components, makes thermal management a critical bottleneck for CPO performance and reliability. We provide a comprehensive review of thermal management in CPO, encompassing various aspects from device assembly to system operation. We systematically discuss the packaging strategies and thermal reliability of lasers and fiber arrays, address thermal design considerations at both chip and package levels, and evaluate advanced thermal interface materials alongside module-level cooling technologies. Finally, we provide perspectives on future optoelectronic co-design and the thermal challenges of next-generation optical interconnects.

sources.title: Silicon Photonics for Co‐Packaged Optics: A Review of Core PIC Components and Industry Strategies
sources.abstract: ABSTRACT Co‐packaged optics (CPO) has emerged as a pivotal technology for overcoming the bandwidth, power, and scalability bottlenecks of next‐generation AI and data center interconnects by closely integrating the optical engine (OE) with electronic chips (e.g., ASICs and XPUs). As a key component of the OE, photonic integrated circuits (PIC) are predominantly realized on the silicon photonics (SiPh) platform, which provides CMOS‐compatible fabrication, scalable heterogeneous integration, and the capability to implement full photonic functionalities on chip. Thus, this review presents a comprehensive overview of recent advances in core device‐level components of SiPh‐based PIC, including laser sources, Si‐based modulators, passive optical couplers, Ge‐on‐Si photodetectors, and multiplexers/demultiplexers, which significantly impact the performance of CPO systems. Industry strategies and representative system‐level demonstrations are also summarized to depict the current technological landscape. Furthermore, critical challenges and potential solutions for CPO system development are discussed, such as laser integration, thermal management, device reliability, bandwidth density, and energy efficiency. Together, these insights offer a device‐level roadmap for advancing CPO toward scalable, high‐performance, and economically viable deployment.

sources.title: Glass Substrate for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics leads to significant power reduction by placing the electronic and photonic chiplets in a single package. An integrated electro-optical substrate made of glass with optical waveguides, through vias and electrical redistribution layers inside a single-sided cavity enables fine-line electrical routing and low-cost assembly. Existing glass and thin film technologies were evaluated and combined into a single process stream including photonic assembly. Photonic chips with silicon nitride waveguides were optically coupled to integrated low-loss (<0.1 dB/cm) glass waveguides with minimum loss of 0.65 dB achieved by fiducial alignment and pick-and-place assembly.

sources.title: 3D Heterogeneous Integration of Back-Emitting VCSEL Arrays via Flip-Chip Bonding for Co-Packaged Optics Systems
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
sources.abstract: Flip-chip bonding is a promising technique for integrating Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Lasers (VCSELs) in Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) for high-speed applications, but it requires careful optimization of Gold (Au) bumps bonding parameters to address thermal management, ensure efficient optical coupling, and enhance device performance. This study investigates the packaging performance of a VCSEL array integrated onto silicon interposers using flip-chip bonding with Au bumps under various bonding conditions. Emphasis is placed on the effects of bump flattening and alignment accuracy on bonding quality and overall device performance. Au bumps with flattened surfaces and optimized misalignment were analyzed through SEM imaging, luminescence testing, and L-I-V (Light–Current–Voltage) characterization. Results show that flattening Au bumps and a small misalignment between the two Au bumps significantly improve surface planarity and enhance both electrical and optical performance. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations are also conducted to compare with experimental results and provide further insight into stress distribution and structural behavior. The findings underscore the importance of bump flattening and precise alignment in ensuring mechanical reliability and achieving optimal performance in VCSEL-based optical interconnects for next-generation CPO systems.

findings.claim: Thermal management is repeatedly named as a central constraint on CPO reliability and performance. Co-integrating a high-power-density switch ASIC with temperature-sensitive photonics creates thermal crosstalk and a cooling burden that pluggable optics avoid.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Three independent abstracts, one a 2026 review, agree that thermal management is a bottleneck. They are abstracts only, so the severity cannot be quantified here.
findings.supporting_excerpt: thermal management one of the key challenges that constrain the reliability of high-capacity co-packaged optics

findings.claim: The liquid-cooling evidence is narrow and mostly simulation-backed. The two cooling studies test different bandwidth classes (12.8 Tbps and 51.2 Tbps) with custom cold-plate designs. Agreement is reported as simulation within 4% of a bench platform. The abstracts report no long-term reliability, thermal-cycling, or field data, and no serviceability data for liquid-cooled CPO.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both papers are single-design studies in which simulation and a lab test rig mostly validate each other. The abstracts do not say whether the test vehicles used real operating optical engines or the actual heat loads of a production switch. The reported temperatures (for example an ASIC at 97.3 °C versus optics at 31.3 °C in one study, and 51 °C at 290 W in the other) come from different configurations and cannot be compared. Missing long-term data is a gap, not proof of failure.

findings.claim: Manufacturing yield and alignment precision are acknowledged as unresolved barriers. The VCSEL flip-chip study shows that bonding quality depends on tightly tuned Au-bump flattening and low misalignment, and its validation is lab-scale.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: One review abstract names yield and alignment as open challenges. A device-level study shows that bonding results are sensitive to alignment and bump geometry. The abstracts give no yield percentages, so the scale of the problem is unknown.
findings.supporting_excerpt: thermal management, manufacturing yields, and alignment precision remain key challenges

findings.claim: Standardization and serviceability are open questions that may decide whether CPO moves from early deployment to broad adoption. A 2026 preprint argues that device-centric analyses underweight system-level trade-offs and that CPO is an architectural commitment rather than a component swap.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The main source is an arXiv preprint that is not peer reviewed, and it is a perspective piece rather than an empirical result. The IEEE Communications Magazine abstract only says standardization efforts are 'ongoing', which is consistent with incomplete standards. The horizon is an inference from the phrase 'early deployment'.
findings.supporting_excerpt: standardization, serviceability, and thermal-aware co-design will be decisive in determining whether co-packaged optics can transition from early deployment to widespread adoption

findings.claim: Laser integration, device reliability and the thermal sensitivity of photonic components are listed as unsolved challenges. Fixing the optical engine to the ASIC package means a failed laser or fiber array is harder to replace than a pluggable module, but the abstracts do not quantify this.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The reviews list laser integration, thermal management and device reliability as critical challenges. The replacement-difficulty inference is mine, drawing on the serviceability concern in the preprint. No abstract reports laser failure rates or field reliability data.

findings.claim: Power and bandwidth benefits are described in qualitative terms such as 'significantly reduces' and 'transformative', and the abstracts carry few comparative numbers. Cost and economic viability are named as goals rather than demonstrated. Comparison with near-packaged optics (NPO) is mentioned, but no outcome appears in the abstracts, so displacement risk cannot be assessed.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Several review abstracts use promotional framing without quantified power-per-bit, cost or total-cost-of-ownership comparisons. The NPO comparison is only named, not reported. This describes the evidence available in abstracts, not a flaw in the full papers.

findings.claim: The ecosystem depends heavily on a single integration platform (silicon photonics) and on novel packaging materials and processes that are still early-stage. The glass-substrate work reports a minimum 0.65 dB coupling loss from a single process stream in a 2023 proceedings paper.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Reviews describe PICs as predominantly on SiPh and name a few leading companies, which suggests platform and supplier concentration. The abstracts do not analyze supply-chain concentration directly, so this is an inference. The glass substrate result is a small demonstration with no yield or cost data.

hype_flags: 'Transformative' / 'revolutionize' / 'disruptive' (reviews of CPO): promotional wording not backed by quantified comparisons in the abstracts.
'Significantly reduces power consumption': no power-per-bit figures or like-for-like pluggable baselines appear in the abstracts.
'Excellent performance' of liquid-cooled designs: based on simulation plus a single bench test, with no long-term reliability evidence.
'Economically viable' deployment roadmap: cost evidence is not shown in the abstracts.
Widespread adoption framed as a technical inevitability: the preprint (not peer reviewed) argues that standardization, serviceability and system trade-offs could stall deployment.

finding.claim: S2 presents a single vendor prototype as evidence for the 51.2 Tb/s CPO switch. The abstract gives no power, efficiency, yield, thermal, reliability or serviceability data. 'Industry first' is the authors' own claim. A prototype demonstration says little about manufacturability or deployment readiness, and the 'verified_fact' label covers only that the prototype was reported.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract reports only bandwidth and the prototype's existence. It contains no energy-per-bit, yield or reliability figure, and nothing independent supports the 'first' claim. The finding should be read as a capability demonstration, not evidence of maturity.
finding.supporting_excerpt: An industry first prototype system by co-packaging eight engines with switch die that can deliver double the bandwidth of a 25.6Tb/s solution.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 reports the 0.5–0.65 dB coupling loss as the glass platform's performance. Both numbers are 'minimum' (best-case) values, and the two papers appear to describe the same glass-substrate process stream, so they are not independent confirmation. The finding omits the 0.83 dB average fibre-connector loss reported in the same IEEE JSTQE paper, which adds to the total optical path loss. It also omits that the demonstration is a laboratory process, with no yield or reliability data in the abstracts.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The omitted connector loss is larger than the chip-to-glass coupling loss. Quoting only the best chip-to-waveguide figures overstates link-level performance. The 0.5 dB figure is also described as 'minimum loss', i.e. a best case rather than a distribution.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Average connector loss of 0.83 dB was demonstrated with physical contact between fibers and IOX glass waveguides.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 cites src_8bc0d86153 for 'two integration approaches pursued in parallel' (VCSEL-based and silicon photonics). That abstract never mentions VCSELs and instead calls silicon the most promising platform. Only src_e674fc828f supports the dual-approach claim. Other retrieved reviews describe CPO PICs as 'predominantly' silicon photonics, so 'parallel' may overstate how much VCSEL-based CPO is being pursued.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: One of the two citations does not support the claim as written, and a second retrieved review points to silicon-photonics dominance. The finding needs a narrower citation and a note that the approaches are not equally weighted.
finding.supporting_excerpt: silicon platform is the most promising platform for large-scale integration.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S12 treats the lithography comparison as showing nanoimprint to be superior for CPO silicon waveguides. The abstract's evidence is SEM images of line patterns with emphasis on line-edge roughness. It reports no measured numbers, and no yield, overlay, defectivity or throughput data. The claim of advantages in cost and power is asserted, not quantified. The paper is a single-group conference abstract, and its link to CPO-specific requirements is only asserted.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A qualitative SEM comparison of patterning fidelity is weak support for a tool-selection conclusion. Manufacturing readiness cannot be judged from line-edge roughness alone.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We presented SEM images of line patterns using not only conventional exposure tools such as i-line steppers and KrF scanners, but also a nanoimprint lithography tool
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 and S10 report component results that are self-characterised or still in progress. S6's 'record' efficiency is the authors' own claim, with no comparison table or reliability data in the abstract. S10's ferrule is described as under development ('We are developing and evaluating'), and its abstract gives no quantitative performance, so 'reported to avoid' deformation rests on an unquantified statement. Neither finding should carry the weight of a verified performance result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Both are short conference abstracts from single groups. The S6 efficiency comes from one operating point (100 mW per channel at 55 °C housing temperature). The S10 ferrule is a work-in-progress with no numbers, so neither is independently corroborated.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We are developing and evaluating reflow compatible Ceramics Multifiber Ferrule (CMF)
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S1 states CPO's benefits (bandwidth density, energy efficiency) as established. Beyond the Science agent's own caution, the abstracts supplying these benefits are qualitative advocacy ('significantly reduces', 'transformative') with few comparative numbers. A cited abstract compares CPO with near-packaged optics but gives no outcome in the abstract, so displacement risk and the cost case are not assessed. The 'verified_fact' label on S1 covers only that CPO is proposed for this purpose.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: src_8bc0d86153 states that pluggable-optics growth lags traffic as a motivating assertion. src_a072730865 only says it 'compares CPO with Near-Packaged Optics (NPO)', with no result in the abstract. Without quantified comparisons against pluggables or NPO, the efficiency claim is a goal, not an established result.

finding.claim: The findings focus on component and packaging demonstrations and omit the system-level barriers that retrieved risk literature identifies as decisive: thermal management as a 'critical bottleneck' for reliability, manufacturing yield, alignment precision, laser and fibre-array serviceability, and standardization. S7 mentions thermal crosstalk but frames it as a heterogeneous-integration detail from one paper. The set therefore gives an overly optimistic picture of readiness.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Three independent reviews and one preprint name thermal management, yield, alignment and serviceability as open. The retrieved cooling studies are largely simulation-backed lab platforms. The 2026 preprint (src_57b1133fd7) argues that device-centric analyses underweight system trade-offs. It is a single, uncited preprint, so this is a caution, not a settled conclusion.
finding.supporting_excerpt: makes thermal management a critical bottleneck for CPO performance and reliability.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 concludes that CPO is 'not converging on a single architecture'. The cited abstracts list packaging techniques (2D/2.5D/3D, FOWLP, TSV/TGV) but do not say the field is divergent or that these routes compete rather than complement each other. The finding is also partly cited to src_926601ff5d, whose abstract does not list 2D/2.5D/3D or FOWLP.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A list of covered topics in review abstracts does not show absence of convergence. The routes may serve different bandwidth tiers or product generations, and the abstracts give no market or standards evidence either way.

limitations: Analysis uses titles and abstracts only. Full-text details such as test conditions, error bars and cost models were not seen.
One paper (src_34b3ddf46b, Nature Electronics) has no abstract, so it contributes nothing to the findings.
Most papers are reviews or perspectives that summarize other work, so findings are not fully independent.
The retrieved set is small (12 papers) and skews toward thermal management, so other risk areas (security, supply chain, cost, laser reliability, competing architectures) are thinly covered.
One key source (src_57b1133fd7) is an arXiv preprint and not peer reviewed.
No papers directly compare CPO with NPO, pluggable or linear-drive optics on cost or power, so displacement risk is a gap in the evidence rather than a finding.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were reviewed. Full-paper methods, quantitative results and caveats were not read, so some of the problems flagged may be addressed in the full texts.
Several retrieved items have no abstract (src_6e1e90b306, src_bff4d58588, src_34b3ddf46b) or only a slide-title list (src_89eb116049). They could not be used to test the findings.
I did not challenge S8 and S9 because they are hedged and consistent with their abstracts, though both are advocacy or speculative in tone.

No independent evidence on commercial deployment, cost, yield or field reliability was available, so I could not test those claims against external sources. Several challenges are therefore labelled ai_interpretation.

draft.summary: The evidence shows co-packaged optics (CPO) is an active and fast-growing research field [S1][S2], with code-computed research acceleration of 82->149 papers (YoY 81.7%) between 2024 and 2025, and a first vendor prototype reported at 51.2 Tb/s [S2]. Commercial activity is real but currently visible only as company self-descriptions in SEC filings: Marvell [M1], AMD [M2], Amkor [M3], ASE [M4], Coherent [M5], FormFactor [M6], Lumentum [M7] and Veeco [M8] all describe CPO-related products, services or acquisitions, but no filing excerpt in this set demonstrates a named customer adopting CPO. The main uncertainty is technical and system-level: thermal management [R1], manufacturing yield and alignment [R3], and standardization and serviceability [R4] are repeatedly identified as unresolved, and several Science findings are weakened by challenges [C1][C6][C7]. Patent evidence is absent (patent agent did not run), so no patent-momentum rating is possible, and there is no price or timing evidence. Research activity should not be read as commercial success.

themes.name: Co-packaged optics for AI datacenter interconnect

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Evidence for the near term is company portfolio and roadmap statements rather than deployment outcomes: Marvell lists CPO in its custom silicon/interconnect portfolio [M1], Coherent says it sells CPO products into datacenter/communications [M5], Lumentum supplies lasers and packaging for CPO [M7], and Marvell investor materials describe pre-validated optical engines and optical I/O [M9]. A social post claims 2027 will focus on platform qualification and testing [X1] but is an unverified claim. No price/timing data was provided, so near-term timing risk cannot be assessed.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: A prototype 51.2 Tb/s all-optical switch co-packaging eight 6.4 Tb/s optical engines has been reported [S2], and component-level results exist for external lasers [S6] and glass substrates [S4]. However, standardization and serviceability remain open [R4], and the prototype abstract carries no power, yield, thermal or reliability data [C1]. Whether CPO displaces pluggable or near-packaged optics is not resolved in the evidence [R6].

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The cited evidence does not support a long-horizon outcome. High research volume [S1] does not establish commercial success (see limitations), and cost and economic viability are described as goals rather than demonstrated [R6]. The abstracts give no field reliability or long-term serviceability data [R2][R5].

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: CPO is proposed to raise interconnect bandwidth density and energy efficiency by shortening electrical links through advanced packaging [S1], and a prototype has been reported co-packaging eight 6.4 Tb/s optical engines into a 51.2 Tb/s switch [S2]. Multiple large public companies already describe CPO products or capabilities [M1][M5][M7], AMD made strategic acquisitions for photonics and CPO [M2], and Marvell's investor materials describe pre-validated optical engines and optical I/O for custom XPUs [M9].

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: CPO is developing with real component and packaging progress [S4][S6], commercial activity concentrated in company portfolios and roadmaps [M1][M5][M7], and continued technical work on platform qualification and testing [X1]. Adoption is likely gated by unresolved standardization, serviceability and system-level trade-offs, and CPO is characterised as an architectural commitment rather than a component swap [R4].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The 51.2 Tb/s prototype is a single vendor demonstration with no power, efficiency, yield, thermal, reliability or serviceability data, and 'industry first' is the authors' own claim [C1]. The CPO benefits are described in qualitative advocacy terms with few comparative numbers, and cost and economic viability are goals rather than demonstrations [C6][R6]. Laser integration, device reliability and photonic thermal sensitivity are unsolved, and fixing the optical engine to the ASIC package makes a failed laser or fiber array harder to replace [R5].

catalysts.label: unverified_claim
catalysts.text: Reporting of platform qualification and faster testing/passive alignment would strengthen the near-term case, but this is currently only an unverified social claim [X1].

catalysts.label: ai_interpretation
catalysts.text: Further strategic acquisitions for photonics/CPO, as AMD reported [M2], or Marvell's described optical I/O and external-laser engine push [M9], indicate continued industry investment.

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Thermal management is repeatedly named as a central constraint: co-integrating a high-power-density switch ASIC with temperature-sensitive photonics creates thermal crosstalk and a cooling burden pluggable optics avoid [R1].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Manufacturing yield and alignment precision are acknowledged as unresolved barriers, and the VCSEL flip-chip validation is lab-scale [R3].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Laser integration, device reliability and thermal sensitivity of photonics are listed as unsolved, with harder serviceability than pluggable modules [R5].

risks.label: ai_interpretation

themes.name: Advanced packaging, materials and test supply chain for CPO

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Several companies describe packaging, test or equipment roles today: Amkor positions CPO and silicon photonics wafer-level packaging [M3], ASE lists CPO processing among advanced packaging services and makes optical engines [M4], FormFactor's Keystone Photonics supplies optical probing for CPO/NPO test [M6], and Veeco sees hyperscalers advancing toward near-package and co-packaged optics over the longer term, driving InP epitaxy and facet-coating equipment demand [M8]. horizons.label: ai_interpretation

Manufacturing yield and alignment remain unresolved [R3], and the glass work is a laboratory process without yield or reliability data [C2].

horizons.label: ai_interpretation

themes.name: Thermal management and reliability as the CPO gating factor

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The evidence identifies thermal management as a repeated central constraint but provides no field or reliability outcome [R1]. There is no near-term timing or price evidence provided.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Liquid-cooling work exists but is narrow and mostly simulation-backed, testing different bandwidth classes with custom cold plates and reporting simulation within 4% of a bench platform; no long-term reliability, thermal-cycling, field or serviceability data is reported [R2]. Micro-ring thermal tuning is described as limited by high static power and severe thermal crosstalk, motivating phase-change-material non-volatile photonics [S8].

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: No finding supports a long-horizon conclusion on thermal solutions; the abstracts report no long-term reliability or field data [R2][R5].

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Thermal constraints are being actively researched and alternatives are proposed, such as phase-change-material non-volatile photonics to reduce the high static power and severe thermal crosstalk of conventional micro-ring thermal tuning [S8]. Solving cooling and reliability would unlock CPO's cited bandwidth-density and energy-efficiency benefits [S1].

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: Thermal management is repeatedly named a central constraint on CPO reliability and performance because a high-power-density switch ASIC sits with temperature-sensitive photonics [R1]. The available cooling evidence is narrow and mostly simulation-backed, with custom cold plates and no long-term reliability, thermal-cycling, field or serviceability data [R2].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The findings focus on component and packaging demonstrations and understate system-level barriers that risk literature calls decisive, including thermal management as a critical bottleneck, yield, alignment, laser/fibre-array serviceability and standardization [C7]. Laser integration, device reliability and photonic thermal sensitivity are unsolved, and a failed laser or fibre array is harder to replace than a pluggable module [R5].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Reporting of long-term reliability, thermal-cycling, field or serviceability data for liquid-cooled or otherwise cooled CPO, which the current abstracts do not provide [R2], would strengthen this theme.

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Thermal crosstalk between electrical and optical domains and the cooling burden are central constraints pluggable optics avoid [R1].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Cooling evidence is simulation-heavy with different bandwidth classes and no field, reliability or serviceability data [R2].

risks.label: ai_interpretation

invalidation_conditions.label: forecast

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
